contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you learned what similarity means. Today: a shortcut for proving two triangles are similar!

The AA (Angle-Angle) Similarity Postulate states that if two angles of one triangle are equal to two angles of another triangle, the triangles are similar — you don't need to check all three angles or any side lengths, since a triangle's angles always sum to 180 degrees, so matching two angles automatically forces the third to match too. Given Triangle A with angles 50° and 60°, and Triangle B with angles 50° and 60°, explain why AA lets you conclude these triangles are similar without checking the third angle or any sides.
You just learned the AA Similarity Postulate! Tomorrow we'll use similar triangles to find missing side lengths.

objectives: Explain why the third angle is automatically determined once two angles match
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's similarity-definition work briefly.
2. Introduce the AA Similarity Postulate and the 180-degree-sum reasoning behind it.
3. Have the child explain why the third angle is automatically determined.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's missing-side-length lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: have the child calculate the third angle directly (180-50-60=70) for both triangles to see they match, before explaining why this will always happen
Ready for more: ask the child why AA is enough for SIMILARITY but SAS/ASA/SSS (from last week) were needed for CONGRUENCE — what's the key difference in what each is proving
This connects directly back to last week's triangle-congruence criteria, contrasting what's needed for similarity vs. congruence
teacherGuide.answerKey: Since a triangle's three angles always sum to 180 degrees, if two triangles already share two equal angles, their third angles must also be equal (180 minus the same two numbers gives the same result) — so checking just two angles is enough to guarantee all three match, making the triangles similar by AA.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Geometry standard G-SRT.3: using the AA criterion to prove triangles similar, continuing this week's similarity thread.
